claims.claim: The European labelling convention used in UK and EU medicine leaflets defines frequency words as fixed bands: very common 1 in 10 or more; common 1 in 100 up to 1 in 10; uncommon 1 in 1,000 up to 1 in 100; rare 1 in 10,000 up to 1 in 1,000; very rare fewer than 1 in 10,000.
claims.supporting_passage: Buchter 2014, Table 1 'European commission nomenclature for communicating frequency of adverse effects of drugs': "Very common (≥1/10) Common (≥1/100 to <1/10) Uncommon (≥1/1000 to <1/100) Rare (≥1/10000 to <1/1000) Very rare (<1/10000) Not known cannot be estimated from the available data". Knapp 2004 abstract: "verbal descriptors suggested by the European Union (EU) such as \"common\" (1-10% frequency) and \"rare\" (0.01-0.1%)"
claims.location: Buchter 2014 Background, Table 1 (PMC full text); Knapp 2004 Abstract (Objective)
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition from the European Commission 1998 readability guideline, carried into later guidance; not a study finding
claims.safe_wording: In a medicine leaflet, 'common' means between 1 in 100 and 1 in 10 people: at most 10 in 100, and often fewer. 'Uncommon' means between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 100. 'Rare' means between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 1,000. 'Very rare' means fewer than 1 in 10,000.
claims.qualifications: 'Up to 1 in 10' is only the upper edge of 'common'; say so. The current EU/UK template wording printed in leaflets (for example 'may affect up to 1 in 10 people') was not opened in this project, so quote the bands, not the leaflet phrase.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the definitions.

numbers.meaning: definition of 'common' (1% to under 10% of people taking the medicine)
definition of 'uncommon'
definition of 'rare'
definition of 'very rare'
definition of 'very common'

claims.claim: In a UK randomised study of 120 adults taking statins, those told constipation was 'common' estimated its likelihood at 34.2% on average, against 8.1% for those told the figure 2.5%; for pancreatitis described as 'rare', estimates were 18% with the word and 2.1% with the number 0.04%.
claims.supporting_passage: "120 adults taking simvastatin or atorvastatin after cardiac surgery or myocardial infarction." "Cardiac rehabilitation clinics at two hospitals in Leeds, UK." "Within each side effect condition half the patients were given the information in verbal form and half in numerical form (for constipation, \"common\" or 2.5%; for pancreatitis, \"rare\" or 0.04%)." "The mean likelihood estimate given for the constipation side effect was 34.2% in the verbal group and 8.1% in the numerical group; for pancreatitis it was 18% in the verbal group and 2.1% in the numerical group."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults on statins after cardiac events, Leeds / written statement giving side-effect frequency as a word / same frequency as a percentage / estimated likelihood of the side effect / measured immediately
claims.safe_wording: In a UK study, 120 people taking a statin read that constipation was a 'common' side effect. On average they guessed about 34 in 100 people would get it. People given the actual figure, 2.5 in 100, guessed about 8 in 100. For a 'rare' side effect (4 in 10,000), the word led to an average guess of 18 in 100.
claims.qualifications: Small study; allocation not concealed; estimates were made immediately after reading one statement, so the study shows how the words are read, not what people later did. Even the group given numbers overestimated (8.1% against 2.5%): say this plainly.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with the Buchter 2014 meta-analysis (C06-11-d).

numbers.meaning: participants, adults taking simvastatin or atorvastatin, Leeds
mean estimated likelihood of constipation when told 'common' (verbal group)
mean estimate when told 2.5% (numerical group)
stated frequency of constipation used in the study
mean estimate of pancreatitis when told 'rare'
mean estimate of pancreatitis when told 0.04%
stated frequency of pancreatitis (4 in 10,000)

claims.claim: The frequency words were associated with more negative views of the medicine than the equivalent numbers.
claims.supporting_passage: Knapp 2004: "The verbal descriptors were associated with more negative perceptions of the medicine than their equivalent numerical descriptors." Berry 2003: "In all studies it was found that people significantly over-estimated the likelihood of adverse effects occurring, given specific verbal descriptors. This in turn resulted in significantly higher ratings of their perceived risks to health and significantly lower ratings of their likelihood of taking the medicine."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C06-11-b; Berry 2003 summarises the same group's studies in public, patients and doctors
claims.safe_wording: People given the words also rated the medicine more negatively, and in related studies said they were less likely to take it.
claims.qualifications: Stated intentions on a rating scale, measured once; no study measured whether people actually stopped their medicine.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No behavioural outcome data (Buchter 2014 notes this gap).

claims.claim: A systematic review of 10 randomised trials found that verbal frequency words consistently led to overestimation of side-effect risk; numbers also led to overestimation but less.
claims.supporting_passage: "Ten trials were included. Participants perceived probabilities presented in verbal terms as higher than in numeric terms: commonly used verbal descriptors systematically led to an overestimation of the absolute risk of adverse effects (Range of means: 3% - 54%). Numbers also led to an overestimation of probabilities, but the overestimation was smaller (2% - 20%)." Results: "MD for common side effects: -35.36 [CI: -39.92 to -30.81]". "Only between 9% and 50% of the participants in the numerical groups gave a correct probability for the adverse effects". Limitations: "Many studies were conducted with healthy volunteers and used fictional scenarios." "All outcomes were measured shortly after distribution of the information leaflets, and none of the studies had a follow-up."
claims.location: Abstract (Results); Results (Estimation of probabilities); Description of studies; Limitations of the included studies
claims.pico_timeframe: Mostly general-public volunteers, hypothetical leaflets / verbal EU descriptors / numerical frequency / estimated probability / immediate
claims.safe_wording: Across 10 trials, people given the leaflet words overestimated the chance of a side effect every time. People given numbers also overestimated, but by less.
claims.qualifications: Mostly volunteers reading made-up leaflets; all trials from two UK research groups; measured immediately; no data on behaviour. For 'common' side effects the average overestimate with words was about 35 percentage points larger than with numbers: if used, call it percentage points.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: One trial suggested adding the word to the number may dilute the benefit of the number (post hoc, single trial of 100 people).

numbers.meaning: randomised trials in the review (19 comparisons, 2,145 observations for probability estimates)
range of mean estimates with verbal descriptors across comparisons
range of mean overestimation with numbers
pooled mean difference (verbal higher than numeric) for 'common' side effects
share of numeric-group participants who gave the correct probability

claims.claim: Current EU guidance on leaflets pairs the frequency word with a number, rather than the word alone.
claims.supporting_passage: Buchter 2014 Discussion: "Different preferences imply that using a combined verbal and numerical format may be the best compromise to suit various needs. This is also reflected in the current European Commission Guideline on readability from 2009 as well as the current EU template for patient leaflets". Also: "One study examined a combination of a verbal and numerical description, as it is currently included in the 2009 European Commission Guideline on the readability of package leaflets". EMA search extract (not opened): user testing showed double-sided expressions such as "affects more than 1 in 100 but less than 1 in 10" are not well understood and should not be used in package leaflets.
claims.location: Buchter 2014 Discussion and Description of studies; EMA QRD search extract
claims.pico_timeframe: Regulatory guidance as described in 2014
claims.safe_wording: Many leaflets now print a number beside the word. The Leeds study tested the word alone, so it shows what the word on its own conveys.
claims.qualifications: Do not claim leaflets use words only. The exact current leaflet phrase was not verified.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether the combined word-plus-number format fully fixes the overestimate is uncertain (one trial).

claims.claim: About 1 in 7 older people living at home report difficulty swallowing their medicines, and modifying medicines is common when older people are given them, though the evidence base is small.
claims.supporting_passage: "Five studies met the inclusion criteria. The results suggest that approximately 14 % of community-dwelling older patients experience difficulty swallowing medicines. Between one quarter and one third of occasions of medicine administration to older patients involve the modification of oral medicines." "Difficulty swallowing oral medicines and the modification of medicines are reported as being common issues in the older cohort. However, evidence to support such contentions is limited."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older patients in community and care settings / difficulty swallowing medicines; modification of oral medicines / studies to November 2014
claims.safe_wording: About 1 in 7 older people living at home say they have difficulty swallowing their medicines. Where older people are given medicines by staff, tablets are altered (crushed, split or opened) at between a quarter and a third of doses.
claims.qualifications: Based on only five studies; the authors call the evidence limited.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Schiele 2013 found swallowing difficulty was more common in younger than older primary care patients (C06-01-b), so do not say it is mainly a problem of old age.

numbers.meaning: community-dwelling older patients reporting difficulty swallowing medicines (about 1 in 7)
share of medicine administrations to older patients that involved modifying the medicine
studies included

claims.claim: Difficulty swallowing tablets is often not known to the doctor, and many affected people alter their medicines themselves.
claims.supporting_passage: Schiele 2013: "Of all participants (N = 1,051), 37.4 % reported having had difficulties in swallowing tablets and capsules. The majority (70.4 %) of these patients was not identified by their GP. The occurrence of swallowing difficulties was related to gender (f>m), age (young>old), dysphagia [adjusted odds ratio (adOR): 7.9; p < 0.0001] and mental illness (adOR: 1.8; p < 0.05)." "Because of these difficulties, 58.8 % of the affected patients had already modified their drugs in a way that may alter safety and efficacy and 9.4 % indicated to be non-adherent." "One in 11 primary care patients had frequent difficulties in swallowing tablets and capsules while GPs grossly underestimated these problems." Mc Gillicuddy 2019: "However, when challenges arise, they tend to feel resigned to coping within the constraints of the current medication regimen, resulting in a lack of focused communication with healthcare professionals. Thus, healthcare professionals were unaware of their difficulties and unable to offer advice or solutions."
claims.location: Schiele 2013 Abstract (Results, Conclusions); Mc Gillicuddy 2019 Abstract (Results)
claims.pico_timeframe: German general practice patients of all adult ages on regular tablets (survey); Irish older adults and carers (interviews)
claims.safe_wording: In a survey of 1,051 patients in German general practices, 1 in 11 had frequent trouble swallowing tablets, and GPs had not recognised 7 in 10 of those with any difficulty. More than half of those affected had already altered their tablets themselves. Older people and carers interviewed in Ireland described coping quietly rather than raising it.
claims.qualifications: The survey was of all adult ages and difficulty was commoner in younger patients. Self-report. Avoid 'quietly' (banned word) in the post: use 'without telling anyone' or similar.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None directly conflicting.

numbers.meaning: survey participants, 11 general practices, Germany
reported ever having difficulty swallowing tablets or capsules
primary care patients with frequent difficulty
of those with difficulty, not identified by their GP

claims.claim: Crushing a slow-release (modified-release) tablet can release the dose all at once and cause overdose; crushing a tablet with a stomach-acid-resistant coating is likely to make it underdose.
claims.supporting_passage: "The clinical consequences for the patient of crushing tablets or opening capsules can be serious: alteration of the drug's absorption can result in sometimes fatal overdose, or conversely underdosing, rendering the treatment ineffective. When it disrupts a drug's sustained-release properties, the active ingredient is no longer released and absorbed gradually, resulting in overdose. When a gastro-resistant layer is destroyed by crushing, underdosing is likely." "In practice, there are many drugs that should never be crushed or opened."
claims.pico_timeframe: Review of evidence on crushing tablets or opening capsules, all patients
claims.safe_wording: Crushing a slow-release tablet (often marked MR, SR or XL) destroys the slow release, so the dose is absorbed at once and can cause an overdose. Crushing a tablet with a coating that protects it from stomach acid can stop it working properly. Some medicines should never be crushed or opened.
claims.qualifications: The review describes mechanisms and case harms, not how often harm follows. The label abbreviations (MR, SR, XL) are common examples, not a complete list; the post should say 'often marked'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Another form of the medicine, or another medicine, is sometimes a better solution than crushing; pharmacists are well placed to advise.
claims.supporting_passage: Prescrire 2014: "Before crushing a tablet or opening a capsule, it is better to consider and research the impact it will have on the drug's effects. It is sometimes preferable to use a different dosage form, or a different active ingredient." Mc Gillicuddy 2019: "Whilst the input and expertise of all healthcare professionals will be required, as medication experts, the pharmacy profession should take ownership and become the champion of, and for, the patient."
claims.pico_timeframe: Review and qualitative study; recommendation rather than trial evidence
claims.safe_wording: Before crushing, ask a pharmacist. There may be a liquid, a dispersible tablet or a different medicine that avoids crushing altogether.
claims.qualifications: Do not promise that an alternative always exists ('sometimes' / 'may be'). Naming specific alternatives (liquid, dispersible) is general knowledge consistent with Prescrire's 'different dosage form'; avoid naming patches as a routine alternative. The candidate's pharmacy guidance sources (SPS, NEWT) were not opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Slow-release tablets should not be split, but for most other tablets the evidence gives little support to concerns about splitting (apart from physical difficulty splitting them).
claims.supporting_passage: "No substantive evidence was found to support concerns regarding loss of mass, weight variability, chemical instability, or non-compliance. Evidence does support some older adults struggling to split tablets without tablet splitters, and the inappropriateness of splitting sustained-release preparations, given the potential for alteration of the rate of drug release for some products." "With the exception of sustained-release tablets, which should not be split, and excepting those older people who may struggle to split tablets based on physical limitations, there is little evidence to support tablet-splitting concerns."
claims.pico_timeframe: Systematic review of 138 articles on tablet splitting
claims.safe_wording: Splitting is a different matter from crushing: many tablets can be halved safely, but slow-release tablets should not be split. If in doubt, ask the pharmacist.
claims.qualifications: This corrects the candidate's position: do not say 'no tablet should be split'. No studies were found on splitting enteric-coated tablets.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Manufacturer and pharmacy guidance may still advise against splitting particular products.

claims.claim: In an observational study in English care homes with nursing, medicine administration errors were observed in 57.3% of administrations for residents with swallowing difficulty and 30.8% for residents without.
claims.supporting_passage: "A pharmacist specialised in dysphagia observed nurses during drug rounds and compared these practices with national guidelines. Deviations were classified as types of medication administration errors (MAEs)." "Overall, 738 administrations were observed from 166 patients of which 38 patients (22.9%) had dysphagia. MAE rates were 57.3% and 30.8% for PWD and those without respectively (p<0.001)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Care homes with nursing, North Yorkshire / residents with dysphagia / residents without / deviations from national guidance during observed drug rounds / single observation period
claims.safe_wording: In a small study in English nursing homes, a pharmacist watched drug rounds. Deviations from national guidance occurred at more than half of observed doses for residents with swallowing difficulty (57 in 100), against about 31 in 100 for other residents.
claims.qualifications: Small convenience sample; one observer; 'error' means any deviation from national guidance, not necessarily harm. The abstract calls these 'MAE rates'; full text not opened, so keep the denominator general ('observed doses' or 'observed administrations') and say it was a small study.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Background figures in the abstract (69.5% exposed to errors; 50% with dysphagia) are from other sources and must not be cited as this study's findings.

numbers.meaning: error rate in observed administrations, residents with dysphagia
error rate in observed administrations, residents without dysphagia
administrations observed
residents observed, 38 with dysphagia

claims.claim: Giving medicine hidden in food or drink without the person's knowledge (covert administration) is a different act from crushing with the person's agreement, and raises legal and ethical issues; in UK practice it is preceded by a capacity assessment and best-interests decision.
claims.supporting_passage: Cleary 2026: "Covert medication administration refers to administrating medication in a disguised way without the knowledge of the person receiving it. This practice occurs among vulnerable groups, including children, people with intellectual disabilities, people experiencing mental ill-health, and older people, particularly those living with dementia." Majkic 2025: "The covert administration of medicines is associated with multiple legal and ethical issues." "Pilot audit results showed that 95% of patients receiving covert administration (= 41/43) had evidence of a completed mental capacity assessment and best interests meeting."
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition; UK mental health trust pilot audit
claims.safe_wording: Crushing a tablet into food with the person's agreement is different from hiding medicine in food without their knowledge. Hiding it is called covert medication, and it needs a formal decision about the person's capacity and best interests.
claims.qualifications: The audit shows what UK services do, not the law itself; the Mental Capacity Act and NICE care-home guidance were not opened. Keep to 'needs a formal decision' rather than citing legislation. Crushing for covert use also still needs the pharmacist check.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Scotland uses the Adults with Incapacity Act; wording 'formal decision' covers both.

claims.claim: A used fentanyl patch still contains a substantial amount of drug after its wearing period, enough to harm a child.
claims.supporting_passage: Marquardt 1995: "Nine patches were applied and removed by hospice nurses after 3 days of continuous use on hospice patients with cancer." "Analysis showed 0.7-1.22 mg remaining in the 2.5-mg patches and 4.46-8.44 mg remaining in the 10.0-mg patches. These numbers represent 28-84.4% of the original contents." Hilado 2020: "This case highlights the dangers of not properly disposing of used fentanyl patches as they may still contain enough fentanyl to cause respiratory failure and subsequent unintentional death in children." Finlay and Dunne 2019: "Discarded patches may still contain 50% of original drug -enough to cause serious harm/death"
claims.location: Marquardt 1995 Abstract; Hilado 2020 Abstract; Finlay and Dunne 2019 abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Used patches after 3 days' wear; case report; literature summary
claims.safe_wording: A strong pain patch still contains a substantial amount of medicine after it has been worn for its full time, enough to seriously harm a child or a pet.
claims.qualifications: Do not quote the 28% to 84% range as current: it comes from 9 older-design patches in 1995. The '50%' figure is from a conference abstract summary. Keep to 'a substantial amount'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Residual amount varies by patch design and by person.

numbers.meaning: fentanyl left in 9 used 1995-design patches after 3 days (do not use as a current figure)

claims.claim: Heat over a fentanyl patch increases the amount of drug absorbed, and heat exposure has been identified by the UK regulator as a factor in unintentional overdose.
claims.supporting_passage: Ashburn 2003: "This was an open, 3-period, crossover study that evaluated the pharmacokinetics and safety of 25 microg/h transdermal fentanyl administered with and without local heat." "However, significant differences were seen during the first 4 hours, with C(max) and AUC values almost 3 times higher for the heated administrations than for the administrations without heat." "The addition of heat at 24 hours resulted in rapid increases in serum fentanyl concentrations for both groups". Hilado 2020 (full text): "Skin temperature elevation can lead to a gradual 10-to 15-fold increase in cutaneous blood flow, enhancing the absorption of the transdermal fentanyl [2]." MHRA search extract (not opened): factors possibly related to unintentional overdose include "exposure of the patch to a heat source, possibly resulting in increased fentanyl absorption."
claims.location: Ashburn 2003 Abstract; Hilado 2020 Introduction; MHRA Drug Safety Update (search extract)
claims.pico_timeframe: 10 volunteers / controlled local heat over a 25 microgram/hour patch / no heat / blood fentanyl levels / during and after heating over 30 hours
claims.safe_wording: Heat over a patch makes the skin absorb the medicine faster. In a small study of volunteers, a heating pad over a fentanyl patch raised blood levels to almost 3 times higher during the heated hours. Keep hot water bottles, heat pads and electric blankets off the patch.
claims.qualifications: Small volunteer study with a controlled heating device; over the whole 36 hours the total dose was not significantly different, so describe the effect as a rise during heating. The MHRA wording is a search extract only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No study of hot water bottles or electric blankets specifically; the advice extends the principle.

numbers.meaning: peak blood level and exposure in the first 4 hours with heat compared with no heat (10 volunteers)
volunteers in the heat study

claims.claim: Heat over a buprenorphine patch has also been shown to increase blood levels.
claims.supporting_passage: "Application of external heat using a heating pad over buprenorphine transdermal system, Butrans® has been shown to increase systemic levels of buprenorphine in human volunteers."
claims.pico_timeframe: Earlier volunteer study (not opened) summarised in a 2023 laboratory study
claims.safe_wording: The same applies to buprenorphine patches: heat over the patch raised blood levels in volunteers.
claims.qualifications: Second-hand statement from the paper's background; the original clinical study was not opened. Use as a supporting sentence only.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Putting on a new patch without removing the old one is a recognised cause of too-high doses of opioid patches.
claims.supporting_passage: Lovborg 2014 Abstract: "In the study 151 MEs were identified. The three most common error types were wrong administration time 67 (44%), wrong dose 34 (23%), and omission of dose 20 (13%)." Full text (Scite excerpt): "Of the 34 MEs with wrong dose, 13 were cases of too high dose, 10 were cases of too low dose, and 4 with unspecified wrong dose. Of the cases with too high dose, 7 were cases where the old patch were not removed before a new patch was applied." "The second case concerns a patient who received a higher dose than prescribed. At admittance to hospital health care personnel found two sets of patches of the prescribed dose on the patient". "Educating healthcare personnel in transdermal opioid pain management and the importance of carefully checking patient for old patches before applying new ones would likely reduce the risk of overdosing." Lampert 2014: "The systematic investigation of published errors illustrated that every step in the transdermal patch administration process is prone to errors. Thereby, the lack of knowledge and awareness of the importance of a correct administration practice were a major source of risk."
claims.location: Lovborg 2014 Abstract, Results and Discussion (full-text excerpts); Lampert 2014 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Incident reports of fentanyl and buprenorphine patch errors, Swedish region, 2004 to 2011; systematic review of published errors
claims.safe_wording: One of the commonest ways a patch dose ends up too high is simple: the old patch is still on when the new one goes on. In one Swedish region's incident reports, this explained 7 of the 13 reports of too high a dose. Check for the old patch, take it off, and write down where and when the new one went on.
claims.qualifications: Incident reports cannot give how often this happens overall. The site-and-time record is a recommended practice (Lovborg; Lampert), not tested in a trial.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The commonest reported error overall was late changing of patches (44%), not duplication.

numbers.meaning: patch medication errors reported, one Swedish region, 2004 to 2011
too-high-dose reports caused by the old patch not being removed
errors that were wrong administration time (most common type)

claims.claim: Used patches should be folded in half with the sticky sides together before disposal, and disposed of as advised so children and pets cannot reach them.
claims.supporting_passage: Hilado 2020 (full text): "Regarding patch disposal, the FDA has placed fentanyl patches on its \"flush list\" and advises folding them in half and flushing them down the toilet after use. However, it is ideal to hand them over to a drug take-back site where they can be properly discarded [10]." Finlay and Dunne 2019: "Discarded patches should be folded putting the sticky sides of each patch together so that it sticks to itself. They should then be wrapped in paper or plastic before disposal". "Used patches should be disposed of carefully and not be put in a wastepaper bin where pets may find and ingest them". MHRA search extract (not opened): patients and caregivers should follow the instructions on the patch carton and in the accompanying leaflet.
claims.location: Hilado 2020 Discussion; Finlay and Dunne 2019 abstract; MHRA search extract
claims.pico_timeframe: Safety advice (US regulator via case report; UK clinicians' literature review)
claims.safe_wording: Fold a used patch in half, sticky sides together, and dispose of it as the leaflet or pharmacist advises, out of reach of children and pets.
claims.qualifications: Do not advise flushing (US advice). The UK disposal route (for example returning to a pharmacy) was not confirmed from an opened UK document, so say 'as the pharmacist advises'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Disposal routes differ between countries.

claims.claim: Too much opioid from a patch can cause dangerous slowing of breathing; signs to watch for include unusual drowsiness and slow or shallow breathing, and anyone accidentally exposed needs urgent medical help.
claims.supporting_passage: Lovborg 2014: "Harm was reported in 26 (17%) of the included cases, of which 2 (1%) were regarded as serious harm (nausea/vomiting and respiratory depression)." Hilado 2020: "they may still contain enough fentanyl to cause respiratory failure and subsequent unintentional death in children." MHRA search extract (not opened): "Urgent medical attention should be sought for anyone accidentally exposed to a fentanyl patch."
claims.location: Lovborg 2014 Abstract; Hilado 2020 Abstract; MHRA search extract
claims.pico_timeframe: Incident reports; case report; regulatory advice
claims.safe_wording: Watch for unusual sleepiness or slow, shallow breathing. If you see this, or a child or pet has touched or chewed a patch, get urgent medical help.
claims.qualifications: 'Unusual sleepiness' is the standard presentation of opioid excess; the sources name respiratory depression and respiratory failure explicitly. Do not describe confusion (delirium is out of scope). The urgent-help instruction rests on a search extract plus general safety judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Patches are widely used among older people in care homes, and most contain opioids.
claims.supporting_passage: "This was a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of eMAR data from 66 Australian RACFs including 4,787 permanent residents, aged ≥65 years in January 2017." "One in five ( = 937) residents used a patch, and 83.6% of patches contained opioids, a high-risk medicine."
claims.pico_timeframe: Australian residential aged care, January 2017
claims.safe_wording: In 66 Australian care homes, 1 in 5 residents had a medicine patch, and more than 8 in 10 of those patches contained an opioid.
claims.qualifications: Australian data; optional context only; UK figures not found.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: care home residents aged 65+ using a patch (937 of 4,787), Australia 2017
of patches that contained an opioid

claims.claim: Errors in the medicines history taken at hospital admission are common, most often a medicine left off.
claims.supporting_passage: "We identified 22 studies involving a total of 3755 patients (range 33-1053, median 104). Errors in prescription medication histories occurred in up to 67% of cases: 10%- 61% had at least 1 omission error (deletion of a drug used before admission), and 13%- 22% had at least 1 commission error (addition of a drug not used before admission); 60%- 67% had at least 1 omission or commission error." "In 6 of the studies (n = 588 patients), the investigators estimated that 11%-59% of the medication history errors were clinically important." "Improved physician training, accessible community pharmacy databases and closer teamwork between patients, physicians and pharmacists could reduce the frequency of these errors."
claims.pico_timeframe: Hospital admissions / physician-taken prescription medication history / comprehensive history / omission and commission errors / studies to April 2005
claims.safe_wording: When people are admitted to hospital, the list of their medicines is often incomplete. Across 22 studies, between 1 in 10 and 6 in 10 patients had at least one regular medicine left off the admission list.
claims.qualifications: Older review (studies to 2005), prescription medicines only; wide ranges; many hospitals now use pharmacy-led reconciliation, which reduces but does not remove errors. Do not present a single figure as current.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: More recent UK rates not established in this batch.

numbers.meaning: studies, 3,755 patients
patients with at least one omitted medicine on the admission history, range across studies
of history errors judged clinically important (6 studies)

claims.claim: NICE recommends that on admission to hospital the list should include all medicines, including over-the-counter and complementary medicines, with reconciliation within 24 hours, and that patients and families should be involved.
claims.supporting_passage: "Recommendation 1.3.1. In an acute setting, accurately list all of the person's medicines (including prescribed, over-the-counter and complementary medicines) and carry out medicines reconciliation within 24 hours or sooner if clinically necessary, when the person moves from one care setting to another; for example, if they are admitted to hospital" "Recommendation 1.3.6. Involve patients and their family members or carers, where appropriate, in the medicines reconciliation process"
claims.location: Shah and Barnett 2015, abstract text reproducing NICE NG5 recommendations
claims.pico_timeframe: NICE guideline NG5 (2015), England
claims.safe_wording: NICE guidance says the hospital should list all of a person's medicines, including those bought over the counter and herbal or complementary remedies, and should involve the family where appropriate.
claims.qualifications: Secondary reproduction; the NICE page itself could not be opened. NICE applies to England; say 'NICE guidance' rather than 'the law' or 'UK rules'. The 24-hour detail is optional.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: NICE timeframe for medicines reconciliation after admission (or sooner if clinically necessary)

claims.claim: Denosumab for osteoporosis is given as an injection under the skin every 6 months, so it will not be among the boxes of tablets at home.
claims.supporting_passage: "Subjects were randomly assigned to receive either 60 mg of denosumab or placebo subcutaneously every 6 months for 36 months." "Denosumab given subcutaneously twice yearly for 36 months was associated with a reduction in the risk of vertebral, nonvertebral, and hip fractures in women with osteoporosis."
claims.pico_timeframe: FREEDOM trial dosing schedule
claims.safe_wording: Some bone treatments, such as denosumab, are an injection given once every 6 months. Nothing about it will be in the bag of boxes at home, so name it.
claims.qualifications: The 'not in the bag' point is a logical consequence of the dosing, not a study finding. Do not add claims about what happens if it is missed (not researched in this batch).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: denosumab 60 mg injection schedule

claims.claim: About a third of older people taking prescribed medicines also take herbal remedies or supplements, and some of these combinations carry a potential for interactions.
claims.supporting_passage: Agbabiaka 2018: "A questionnaire asking about prescription medications, HMPs, and sociodemographic information was posted to 400 older adults aged ≥65 years, identified as taking ≥1 prescription drug." "In total 155 questionnaires were returned (response rate = 38.8%) and the prevalence of concurrent HMPs and dietary supplements with prescriptions was 33.6%." "The most commonly used dietary supplements were cod liver oil, glucosamine, multivitamins, and vitamin D." "Sixteen participants (32.6%) were at risk of potential adverse drug interactions." "GPs should routinely ask questions regarding herbal and supplement use, to identify and manage older adults at potential risk of adverse drug interactions." Agbabiaka 2017: "Prevalence of concurrent use by older adults varied widely between 5.3 and 88.3%." "Potential risks of bleeding due to the use of Ginkgo biloba, garlic or ginseng with aspirin or warfarin was the most reported herb-drug interaction."
claims.location: Agbabiaka 2018 Abstract (Method, Results, Conclusion); Agbabiaka 2017 Abstract (Results)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 65+ on at least one prescription, two English general practices (survey); systematic review of 22 studies
claims.safe_wording: In a survey of older people in two English general practices, about 1 in 3 who took prescribed medicines also took a supplement or herbal remedy. Some combinations can interact: the most often reported is a raised bleeding risk when ginkgo, garlic or ginseng is taken with aspirin or warfarin.
claims.qualifications: Low response rate (39%) and small sample; 'potential' interactions, not observed harm. Prevalence varies widely between studies, so do not generalise the one-third figure beyond 'in one English survey'. St John's wort interactions were not sourced in this batch; do not name them.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Prevalence ranges from 5.3% to 88.3% across studies.

numbers.meaning: of 155 responding older adults on prescriptions who also used herbal products or supplements (about 1 in 3)
survey response rate (155 of 400)
range of concurrent prescription and herbal use across 22 studies

claims.claim: Medicines prescribed and supplied by a hospital clinic may not appear on the GP record.
claims.pico_timeframe: No UK source found in PubMed, Scite or Drive searches in this batch
claims.safe_wording: Do not state that hospital-supplied medicines are missing from GP records. The post may list 'medicines supplied by a hospital clinic' as an item to name, without claiming anything about GP records.
claims.qualifications: Unsupported as worded.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Plausible and widely believed, but no opened source.

claims.claim: In hospital, Parkinson's medicines are often given late: in one study half of doses were more than 30 minutes late.
claims.supporting_passage: Richard 2022: "A total of 102 admissions of 70 patients (67% men) were included for analysis." "Time-critical medications were prescribed correctly on admission in 50% of admissions, with errors in medication timing most common (31.6%). Of all doses, 51.7% were administered >30 minutes late, and 29.7% of doses were administered >1 hour late." Yu 2023: "The study included 492 patients with 725 admissions." "Of the admission days with known outpatient timing regimens, 47% had an average deviation of more than 30 min and 22% had at least one missed levodopa dose."
claims.pico_timeframe: Unplanned admissions, Dublin, 15 months (per dose); Cleveland Clinic admissions, 12 months (per admission day against the home schedule)
claims.safe_wording: In a Dublin hospital study, half of Parkinson's doses (52 in 100) were given more than 30 minutes late, and about 3 in 10 more than an hour late. In a large US hospital, on nearly half of hospital days the timing was more than 30 minutes away from the person's home schedule, and on about 1 day in 5 a levodopa dose was missed.
claims.qualifications: Single-centre studies outside the UK; the second figure is per hospital day, not per dose. Present each figure with its own denominator.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Rates vary between hospitals; improvement programmes have raised on-time rates (not researched in depth here).

numbers.meaning: doses given more than 30 minutes late, 102 admissions, Dublin
doses given more than 1 hour late, same study
admission days with average timing deviation over 30 minutes from home schedule, 725 admissions, Cleveland
admission days with at least one missed levodopa dose, same study

claims.claim: Missed and mistimed Parkinson's doses in hospital are linked with longer stays and, for omitted doses, higher in-hospital death rates; the studies are observational.
claims.supporting_passage: Lertxundi 2017: "All PD patients admitted to any of the 11 public acute-care hospitals in the Basque Country in 2011-2012 were included." "The study included 1628 patients admitted 2546 times. Medication errors, affecting almost one third of admissions and half of patients, were associated with higher mortality: inappropriately omitted dopaminergic drug doses OR = 1.92 CI 95% (1.34-2.76)" "Inappropriately omitted doses and both inappropriate antipsychotic and antiemetic administration were associated with a significant 4-day increase in median hospital stay." Yu 2023: "LOS was longer with each additional day of over-dose (4%), under-dose (14%), missed dose (21%), timing deviation (15%) and substitution (19%), (all p < 0.0001)." "Deviations between outpatient and hospital regimens, and administration of antidopaminergic medications, were associated with poor outcomes."
claims.location: Lertxundi 2017 Abstract (Methods, Results); Yu 2023 Abstract (Results, Conclusion)
claims.pico_timeframe: Basque public hospitals 2011 to 2012, retrospective; Cleveland Clinic 12 months, retrospective / omitted or mistimed doses / admissions without / length of stay, in-hospital or 90-day mortality
claims.safe_wording: In 11 Spanish hospitals, admissions in which Parkinson's doses were wrongly left out were linked with a median stay about 4 days longer and with higher death rates in hospital. A US study found each extra day with a missed dose or badly timed doses was linked with a longer stay. These studies show a link; they do not prove the late doses caused the longer stays.
claims.qualifications: Observational: sicker people may both miss doses and stay longer. Do not turn the odds ratio (1.92) into 'twice as likely to die'. Per the editor, do not list drugs to avoid: the 'almost one third of admissions' headline includes dopamine-blocking drugs, so if quoted it must be described as 'errors with Parkinson's medicines, including missed doses'; prefer the omitted-dose results. The antipsychotic odds ratio in the abstract has an inconsistent confidence interval and must not be used.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Causation not established; residual confounding likely.

numbers.meaning: people with Parkinson's, 2,546 admissions, 11 Basque public hospitals, 2011 to 2012
longer median hospital stay associated with wrongly omitted doses (association)
of admissions with any medication error (includes dopamine-blocking drugs; use with care)
relative increase in length of stay per additional day with a missed dose (Cleveland; association)
relative increase in length of stay per additional day with timing deviation (Cleveland; association)

claims.claim: Parkinson's medicine schedules are highly individual and time-critical; the NICE standard, as applied in a UK audit, is administration within 30 minutes of the prescribed time.
claims.supporting_passage: Cox 2024: "People with Parkinson's disease require careful administration, titration, adjustment and monitoring of their antiparkinsonian medicines regimen, which is highly individualised." "It is crucial that people with Parkinson's disease take their antiparkinsonian medicines at exactly the right time, since the inaccurate timing of these medicines can have significant adverse health implications." Omer 2025: "The audit was assessed against the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) QS164, NG71, and QS120 standards, which expect 100% accurate prescribing and administration of time-critical PD medicines within ±30 minutes." "Correct administration times fell from 39/50 (78%) to 33/50 (66%)."
claims.location: Cox 2024 Abstract (key points); Omer 2025 Abstract (Methods, Results)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK nursing guidance; single-hospital UK audit, 2023 and 2024
claims.safe_wording: Parkinson's medicine times are set for each person and are time-critical. The standard used in UK hospital audits, based on NICE, is that each dose is given within 30 minutes of the person's prescribed time.
claims.qualifications: The NICE quality standard itself was not opened; the 30-minute standard is as stated by the UK audit authors. Cox 2024 is expert guidance. Do not quote 'crucial' from Cox (banned word in the post's own voice).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: NICE-based standard for giving time-critical Parkinson's doses, as cited by the UK audit
admissions with correct administration times in one English hospital audit (50 admissions per period)

claims.claim: People with Parkinson's prioritise timely doses and autonomy in hospital, and a recent review recommends enabling self-administration where appropriate.
claims.supporting_passage: "Four studies met the inclusion criteria. Four overarching themes reflected the core medication-related priorities of PwP during hospitalisation: timely and accurate medication administration, autonomy, access to skilled and knowledgeable staff, and advocacy to support patient needs." "Findings suggest the need to strengthen systems supporting timely medication administration, enable self-administration where appropriate, promote flexibility and person-centred care, and implement Parkinson's clinical champions to advocate for and support PwP throughout hospitalisation."
claims.pico_timeframe: Qualitative systematic review, 4 studies, search June 2025
claims.safe_wording: People with Parkinson's say that getting doses on time and keeping control of their own medicines are among their top priorities in hospital. A 2026 review recommends that hospitals let people take their own medicines where it is safe to do so.
claims.qualifications: Recommendation based on patients' views (4 studies), not on a trial of self-administration. Phrase as 'ask whether they can keep taking their own', not as a right.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Self-administration is not suitable for everyone (for example when very unwell); the recommendation says 'where appropriate'.

claims.claim: If a person with Parkinson's cannot swallow or is told not to eat or drink, the family should ask for a plan for their Parkinson's medicines rather than accept missed doses.
claims.supporting_passage: Lertxundi 2017: "Inappropriately omitted doses and both inappropriate antipsychotic and antiemetic administration were associated with a significant 4-day increase in median hospital stay." Yu 2023: "22% had at least one missed levodopa dose. LOS was longer with each additional day of ... missed dose (21%)"
claims.pico_timeframe: Observational evidence on omitted doses; the advice itself is a practical judgement
claims.safe_wording: If they cannot swallow, or are told not to eat or drink before a test or operation, ask the team for a plan for the Parkinson's medicines, so doses are not simply missed.
claims.qualifications: Per the editor: say only 'ask for a plan'; do not name patches, conversions or drugs to avoid (C19-22 owns that). The advice is a judgement grounded in the omitted-dose evidence; NICE NG71 text on this was not opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

candidates.reason: Frequency bands confirmed from the European Commission table (Buchter 2014 full text); Knapp 2004 figures confirmed exactly from the abstract (120 statin users, Leeds; 34.2% vs 8.1% for 'common'/2.5%; 18% vs 2.1% for 'rare'/0.04%); the 10-trial meta-analysis confirms the pattern. The post must say 'common' is a band from 1 in 100 up to 1 in 10 (upper edge only 10 in 100), that the numeric group also overestimated, that estimates were immediate and not behaviour, and that current leaflets often add a number beside the word.

All essential claims supported: about 14% of older people at home report difficulty swallowing medicines (small SR); GPs often do not know (Schiele: 70.4% not identified); crushing slow-release tablets can cause overdose and crushing acid-resistant coatings can cause underdosing (Prescrire); ask a pharmacist about another form. Serrano Santos figures confirmed from the abstract (57.3% vs 30.8% of observed administrations; small study). Required wording changes: drop 'no tablet should be split' (only slow-release tablets should not be split; Saran 2022); do not claim licence status; do not use the abstract's background figures; state that swallowing difficulty in the Schiele survey was commoner in younger patients. The sharpen point on covert medication is supported (C06-01-g).

Residual drug (Marquardt 1995; Hilado 2020), heat increasing absorption (Ashburn 2003, almost 3 times higher during heated hours; buprenorphine background in Thomas 2023), old patch left on as a cause of overdose (Lovborg 2014: 7 of 13 too-high-dose reports), fold sticky sides together (Hilado; Finlay and Dunne) and warning signs (respiratory depression) all supported with qualifications. Use 'a substantial amount' rather than a percentage; do not advise flushing; say 'dispose of as the pharmacist advises'; MHRA advice is a search extract only and may serve as the public link alongside the papers.

Admission medicine-history errors (Tam 2005), NICE's instruction to include over-the-counter and complementary medicines and involve families (via Shah and Barnett 2015), denosumab's 6-monthly injection (FREEDOM) and supplement or herbal use in about 1 in 3 older people on prescriptions (Agbabiaka 2018) are supported. The claim that hospital-supplied medicines may be missing from the GP record has no source (C06-15-e, not_found). The St John's wort example was not sourced; use the ginkgo, garlic or ginseng with aspirin or warfarin bleeding example instead, or no named interaction. Timolol is excluded by the editor.
candidates.revised_angle: A list built from the boxes at home misses what is not in the boxes. Name the six-monthly bone injection (denosumab), anything given or supplied by a hospital clinic, and anything bought over the counter, including vitamins and herbal remedies; list eye drops, inhalers, patches and creams as checklist items only. Evidence lines: admission medicine lists often leave medicines off (Tam 2005, older review, give the range); NICE says hospitals should list over-the-counter and complementary medicines too and involve families; about 1 in 3 older people on prescriptions in one English survey also took a supplement or herbal remedy, and some combinations can interact. Make no claim about what the GP record contains. Schedule at least two weeks from C14-19.

candidates.reason: Doses are often late in hospital (Richard 2022: 51.7% of doses over 30 minutes late; Yu 2023: 47% of hospital days more than 30 minutes off the home schedule); missed or mistimed doses are linked with longer stays and omitted doses with higher in-hospital mortality (Lertxundi 2017; Yu 2023; observational); schedules are individual and time-critical, with a NICE-based 30-minute standard (Cox 2024; Omer 2025 audit); patients prioritise autonomy and a 2026 review recommends self-administration where appropriate (Delf and Wright). Follow the editor: keep to own-times dosing and own supply, 'ask for a plan' for nil by mouth, no drug-avoid list, no patches or conversions. Use omitted-dose results from Lertxundi rather than the 'almost one third' headline, which includes dopamine-blocking drugs.
